https://www.dw.com/en/will-russia-start-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ILFE Will Russia start a fresh mobilization drive to bolster the number of recruits? Image: Yevgeny Sofiychuk/TASS/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Russian authorities are planning to "expand mobilization" in autumn this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, citing intelligence services. According to Zelenskyy, Russian President Vladimir Putin is reportedly preparing to recruit additional Russian soldiers to fight in the war against Ukraine . "He is concealing his intention behind different words and signals, but he is making preparations," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that we, together with our partners, exert sufficient pressure on Russia so that the idea of ending this aggression — the idea of peace, rather than further Russian mobilization — prevails," he added. The Ukrainian president also said Russia's army was losing more fighters at the front than it can recruit, even though Putin wants to intensify the attacks and expand the war. Putin issued a decree in autumn 2022 launching a "partial mobilization," which remains in effect to this day, as confirmed by the presidential administration in 2023. The document, it said, "regulates additional measures necessary to ensure that the armed forces fulfill their objectives." Scores of Russians fled abroad after the Kremlin announced a partial mobilization in September 2022 Image: AP/picture alliance What points to a possible new mobilization drive? Independent Russian exile media outlet Verstka and Latvia-based Russian-language news portal Vaschnyje Istorii published an investigative report in late June stating that Russia's leadership was secretly "discussing mobilization" given the difficulties in recruiting new conscripts. One source quoted by Verstka said figures by Moscow ' s mayoral office show the city sent 1,708 people to the front in April of this year and 1,378 in May — around 1,000 fewer people than during the same period last year. This low recruitment rate reportedly continued in June as well. Vaschnyje Istorii reported that the recruitment rate for soldiers serving on fixed-term contracts more than halved in the last quarter of 2025 compared with the same period the previous year. The outlet said the recruitment rate had dropped even further in early 2026. The news outlet also cited sources from different Russian regions revealing that the number of people applying for army contracts was falling. Military personnel interviewed by Verstka said that contract soldiers being sent to fight this year were "unfit for combat," with many new arrivals fleeing the front lines. One conscript told the news outlet that "units are staffed at 30 to 40%, at best." Droves of Russian fighting-age men made also their way to Georgia in 2022 Image: Daro Sulakauri/Getty Images The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported in late July that the Kremlin is laying the groundwork for a fresh mobilization drive. ISW analysts wrote that such a move would be "a personal decision for Putin that is contingent on his personal perception of the battlefield situation and his perception of the stability and integrity of the Kremlin." They added that it "remains unclear whether or how Putin will decide to implement mobilization." A few days ago, Verstka reported that demand for Armenian rental apartments had shot up, driven by Russian interest — just as it had in 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The outlet said rents in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, have risen by about 30% in recent months. According to the report, Russians are planning to leave the country ahead of the State Duma election, scheduled to be held from September 18 to 20. One landlord told the outlet that in recent years most of his clients had been Russians who had already been living in Armenia for quite some time. Now, however, 80% of inquiries were from Russians who had recently moved to Armenia or were planning to relocate there. What has Russia said? Speaking at a press conference in late July, Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov chose not to comment on Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's remarks regarding a possible new mobilization drive, saying "it is not Zelenskyy's job to talk about our plans." Andrei Klishas, a member of the Russian Federation Council, told Russian-language media outlet RTVI in early summer 2026 that a new mobilization was not currently being discussed in the country as it was unnecessary. Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, dismissed rumors about a possible new mobilization, calling them "pre-election propaganda." The former Russian president also claimed that in the first half of 2026, some 200,000 people had enlisted in the Russian army. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has refused to comment on rumors of a looming mobilization Image: Ulf Mauder/dpa/picture alliance "Of course, you can't blindly trust information provided by the Russian authorities," military expert Yan Matveyev told DW. "Information is adjusted to align with their objectives," he added, with regard to Medvedev's statements on the number of new Russian contract soldiers. That said, figures provided by Russian officials are not too far off when compared with analyses by independent researchers, Matveyev said. "Instead of Medvedev's nearly 200,000 new soldiers, that number would probably be closer to 170,000 or 180,000 over six months." In his view, the current recruitment rate is not sufficient for Russia to secure a military victory over Ukraine. A new mobilization drive would not change that, Matveyev added. "Even if they doubled the size of their army, Russia would not be able to defeat Ukraine, but as can be seen from the statements made by Putin and his officials, that is precisely their goal." Matveyev believes that, given the losses on the front lines, the strength of Russia's army will dwindle unless a fresh mobilization is launched. This decline, he believes, will continue slowly at first but then accelerate. "Losses are growing and will continue to rise given current trends." https://www.kyivpost.com/post/81836.text: War Ukraine World North America Latin America Europe Eastern Europe Middle East Africa Asia Economy Business Technology Finance Energy Agriculture Videos Podcasts Analysis Corruption Watch Opinions Culture Reviews History Sports Classifieds Spotlight Cartoons EN UK Lithuania Belarus Lithuania Discovers Underground Tunnel Dug From Belarus to Smuggle Migrants In brief: Lithuanian border guards have discovered an unfinished underground tunnel dug from Belarus beneath the countries’ border fence, allegedly intended to smuggle migrants into Lithuania. The passage, found near Druskininkai, is the third tunnel uncovered by authorities in recent weeks amid growing border security concerns. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 6, 2026, 3:08 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied (Photo: Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Lithuanian border guards have uncovered an underground tunnel dug beneath the country’s border fence with Belarus, allegedly intended for the illegal smuggling of migrants into Lithuania. The tunnel was discovered near the village of Latežeris in the Druskininkai Municipality during a search operation conducted by Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service (VSAT). JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Border guards used specialized equipment provided by their Polish counterparts to locate the passage. The tunnel was dug approximately 1.5 meters underground and reinforced with wooden logs and planks. It stretched about four meters from Belarusian territory beneath the state border into Lithuania. The entrance on the Belarusian side was concealed with camouflage netting. Advertisement However, construction of the tunnel had not been completed, and it was never used for illegal border crossings, VSAT said. After investigators completed procedural work, the tunnel was filled in. Lithuanian authorities said they have recorded 12 attempts to illegally enter the country through underground tunnels since the beginning of 2026. The discovery marks the third tunnel found by the Varėna Border Guard Unit in recent weeks. On July 23, officers uncovered a roughly 5-meter-long tunnel near the village of Pieščiai. Three days later, on July 26, another unfinished tunnel was discovered near the village of Pertakas. That passage extended about 11 meters and contained wooden logs, excavated sand, and buckets. Other Topics of Interest Latvia Closes Belarus Border Latvia temporarily closed its border with Belarus on Friday evening following an information system failure at the Pāternieki border checkpoint. Under Lithuanian law, illegal border crossing can result in a fine, arrest, or imprisonment of up to two years, depending on the circumstances. Lithuania has faced increased security concerns along its border with Belarus amid ongoing migration pressure and accusations that Minsk has facilitated illegal crossings into the European Union. The country also plans to relocate emergency stockpiles of food, fuel, and other essential supplies farther from the Belarusian border to safer areas by 2027. https://www.azernews.az/analysis/263776..text: From Paris to Vilnius, the matryoshka politics of old divisions [OPINION] 12 September 2026 18:15 (UTC+04:00) Elnur Enveroglu Read more The Russians have a rather amusing and mind-bogglingly peculiar doll, famous under its own name: the russkiy matryoshka . Whenever you lift the lid of one, another identical doll emerges from inside. The peculiar feature of this strange toy is that, no matter how many times you take it apart, the replicas never seem to end. Political figures who have defended the Armenian diaspora and separatist elements throughout the former Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict, both in the past and today, bear a striking resemblance to this Russian nesting doll. Wherever you go, you encounter another figure cut from the same cloth. It makes little difference whether it is France, Lithuania or the other side of the Atlantic. They are bound together by the same mould, the same ideological reflexes and, more often than not, the same political cause. Take, for instance, Lithuania’s former foreign minister, Gabrielius Landsbergis. Image: Julius Kalinskas / ELTA Interestingly, the French ambassador to Lithuania, Lucie Stepanyan, has awarded former Lithuanian foreign minister Gabrielius Landsbergis the Knight’s Cross of the French Legion of Honour. The decision is particularly noteworthy given Landsbergis’s position on the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict during his tenure as Lithuania’s foreign minister. Under Landsbergis, Lithuania was among the European countries that openly supported Armenia and adopted positions favourable to Armenian separatist forces in the Karabakh region of Azerbaijan. In 2024, Landsbergis made a number of anti-Azerbaijani statements at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. A year earlier, he announced that Lithuania would provide €350,000 in humanitarian aid to Armenia for people who had left Karabakh. Against this backdrop, France’s decision to honour Landsbergis raises questions about the political message behind the award, particularly given France’s own controversial approach to the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict. Of course, such honours promoted and circulated by the Armenian diaspora are hardly unprecedented. On the contrary, awards granted for such services, as in the case of the former Lithuanian foreign minister, have a familiar ring to them. There has been no shortage of political figures in the European Parliament who, in return for money and expensive gifts, as well as figures in the US Congress during the Biden administration and before, who turned the institutions of politics into a marketplace of influence, have openly championed such causes. There were many members of Congress who received certificates from an organisation known as ANCA and who went to extraordinary lengths to defend Armenia’s political narrative despite being oblivious to the country's geographical position. It is well known that material interests have always played a powerful role in political groupings. Some seek to secure their electoral base, others to climb the political ladder, while others seek to surround themselves with powerful defenders on the political stage. Without necessarily delving deeply into the ideology behind the causes they champion, they defend the ambitions of those who can advance their own political interests. What is disappointing, however, is that such people pursue this course without considering the image and long-term interests of their own countries. Lithuania is a case in point. By taking an openly anti-Azerbaijani line at the level of its foreign ministry after Azerbaijan's tremendous victory over separatism and occupation, it left a stain on its relationship with Azerbaijan. Gabrielius Landsbergis may have left office, but the mark he left behind has not been erased. Today, from official Brussels to Washington, Azerbaijan’s legitimate position is increasingly being acknowledged and defended, yet the scars left behind remain part of the historical record as a diplomatic miscalculation by a country such as Lithuania. As for Lucie Stepanyan, it is increasingly difficult to escape the impression that she has failed to represent France in a manner befitting the office she holds. Her position appears to be marked less by an effort to encourage reconciliation and more by a persistent defence of separatist narratives and attempts to breathe new life into a conflict that Armenia and Azerbaijan have already begun to leave behind. Indeed, for such an initiative, it would almost be fitting to bestow upon Lucie Stepanyan the title of goddess of war. It is no coincidence that Stepanyan was also awarded the silver grade of the Medal of Honour of France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs for her services following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine. A comprehensive look at this diplomat’s career makes one thing abundantly clear: her interest in conflicts runs remarkably deep. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/30/russ.text: "We have been killed," reads a statement from the editorial team behind the Russian independent news outlet Novaya Gazeta, as it announced on Friday that it would be ceasing operations."On November 9th, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave," the paper said. "The newspaper no longer exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations."The paper is one of the few Russian outlets that has been openly critical of Russia's war in Ukraine, but it has come under increasing pressure from Moscow, which revoked its media licence in 2022 and has detained its journalists.The outlet said its team were now also being evicted from its headquarters on Potapovsky Lane in Moscow and that the donations platform it used to receive financial support from readers had also been closed down."We have been stripped of all our resources. Entirely," it said, calling it a "coordinated campaign.""Banks which have cut us off tell us they are merely following internal corporate rules. They don’t tell us that the rules they follow are set by the FSB, the state security service, embedded in every organsiation. They see the country as their personal fiefdom," the statement continued.It added that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, it had been unable to report on the "most critical and tragic events of our time" and that censorship applied to "virtually every sphere of civic life."One final issue of the paper is still set to be published, however.Independent Russian journalists have issued a statement in support of Novaya Gazeta."The story of the most important independent publication in modern Russia has come to an end. Novaya was a unique newspaper from the moment it was founded right up to the very end. There is not a single other newsroom on the market with such a curriculum vitae: this refers both to the list of phenomenal investigations and outstanding texts, and to the list of awards, including Dmitry Muratov's Nobel Prize, and to the list of murdered journalists," a text published by the Meduza outlet reads."By all measures this was the best media outlet in the history of Russia," it added.Along with the newsroom, the museum of journalist Anna Politkovskaya is also closing; it was opened in her office on 7 October 2021, on the 15th anniversary of her murder.Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 by Sergei Kushnerev, Pavel Voshchanov, Akram Murtazaev, Dmitry Sabov and Dmitry Muratov.The editorial office's first computers were purchased with the help of former USSR president Mikhail Gorbachev.At the end of March 2022, after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, Novaya suspended its work due to warnings from media monitoring agency Roskomnadzor but later resumed operations.After the start of the war, some of its journalists left Russia and set up Novaya Gazeta Europe, which has its main office in Latvia.
